lead: Pandas is a Python library for labelled tables. A Series is one labelled column; a DataFrame is a table with row labels (the index) and column names. Labels let you select, clean, group and join data by name instead of by position. A shop can keep items, prices and quantities in one DataFrame and compute bills by column. Some syllabi call this data frames or data wrangling.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 dictionaries and lists, and 6.1 NumPy arrays for column-wise arrays.

sections.h3: Series and DataFrame from lists and dictionaries

blocks.text: Import pandas as pd. A Series stores one-dimensional data plus an index. pd.Series([78,45,90]) gives positions 0, 1, 2. pd.Series([78,45,90], index=['Asha','Bilal','Chen']) gives labels. A DataFrame stores two-dimensional data: many Series sharing one row index. Build from a dictionary of lists: keys are column names, lists are column values, and the index argument sets row labels. Build from a list of dictionaries: each dictionary is one row; missing keys become NaN. The .index holds row labels; .columns holds column names; .values gives the underlying NumPy array (see 6.1).
Use a dictionary when columns are already separate lists. Use a list of dictionaries when rows arrive one by one, such as records read from a CSV file. Both forms become the same table.

items: A Series has one name; a DataFrame has many column names.
Labels can be strings, dates or numbers; positions are always 0, 1, 2, ....
A DataFrame column is a Series with the same index.

sections.h3: Inspect, select, filter, add and sort

blocks.text: df.head() shows the first five rows; df.head(2) shows two. df.info() lists column names, non-null counts and data types. df.describe() gives count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and maximum for numeric columns. These three checks catch wrong column names, missing values and impossible numbers before calculation.

Selection has two tools. df.loc[row_label, column_label] uses labels. df.iloc[row_position, column_position] uses integer positions. df.loc['Asha':'Chen'] includes both end labels. df.iloc[0:2] returns positions 0 and 1 and excludes 2. A single label returns a Series; a list of labels returns a DataFrame.

Boolean filtering keeps rows where a condition is true: df[df['Math'] >= 50]. Combine conditions with & (and), | (or), and put each condition in parentheses. Add a column by assignment: df['Total'] = df['Math'] + df['Sci']. Sort with df.sort_values('Total', ascending=False); the default is ascending. For assignment to part of a table, use one .loc: df.loc[df['Math'] >= 50, 'Total'] = 0. Chained indexing such as df[df['Math'] >= 50]['Total'] = 0 may edit a copy and fail.

df.isna() returns True where a value is missing. df.fillna(0) replaces missing values with 0; df.dropna() removes rows with any missing value. Both return a new DataFrame unless you assign the result or pass inplace=True. Check the count first with df.isna().sum(); filling every gap with 0 can hide a bad record.

df.groupby('Class')['Total'].mean() splits rows by each class, computes the mean Total in each group, and combines the answers into a Series indexed by class. The split-apply-combine idea replaces manual loops. You can use .sum(), .count(), .max() or .agg(['mean','max']).

pd.merge(left, right, on='Roll', how='inner') joins two DataFrames on a key column. how='inner' keeps matching keys; 'left' keeps all left keys; 'outer' keeps all keys. This is the table join from SQL, now with labels. Use small tables: pandas is comfortable with thousands of rows, not millions.

spec.title: marks DataFrame
spec.aria: A marks table with rows Asha, Bilal and Chen and columns Math, Sci and Total; Total is the row sum.

examples.question: Given df = pd.DataFrame({'Math':[78,45,90],'Sci':[82,50,88]}, index=['Asha','Bilal','Chen']), add Total = Math + Sci, select rows with Math ≥ 50, and give the mean Total of the selected rows.
steps: Math values are 78, 45, 90; Sci values are 82, 50, 88; row labels are Asha, Bilal, Chen.
Asha Total = 78 + 82 = 160. Bilal Total = 45 + 50 = 95. Chen Total = 90 + 88 = 178.
Test Math ≥ 50: Asha 78 passes, Bilal 45 fails, Chen 90 passes. Selected rows are Asha and Chen.
Selected Totals are 160 and 178. Sum = 160 + 178 = 338. Count = 2. Mean = 338 ÷ 2 = 169.
examples.answer: The mean Total of the selected rows is 169 marks.
examples.check:
math = [78, 45, 90]
sci = [82, 50, 88]
names = ['Asha', 'Bilal', 'Chen']
totals = [m + s for m, s in zip(math, sci)]
for t in totals:
    print(t)
selected = [t for m, t in zip(math, totals) if m >= 50]
print(int(sum(selected) / len(selected)))

traps: loc includes the end label; iloc excludes the stop position. df.loc[0:2] can mean labels 0, 1, 2, while df.iloc[0:2] means positions 0 and 1.
Chained indexing for assignment may change a temporary copy. Use df.loc[condition, 'column'] = value or df['column'] = ....
fillna and dropna return new objects by default; without assignment the original table is unchanged.
A DataFrame column is a Series; selecting a list of columns with df[['Math']] returns a DataFrame, but df['Math'] returns a Series. The double brackets are not a typo.
In Boolean filters use & and |, not and and or, and keep parentheses around each comparison.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a Series and a DataFrame?
quiz.a: A Series is one-dimensional and labelled; a DataFrame is two-dimensional with a row index and column names.

quiz.q: Why does pandas give rows an index?
quiz.a: The index labels rows so selection, alignment and grouping work by name, not only by position.

quiz.q: For df with Math values [78,45,90] and index Asha, Bilal, Chen, what does df[df['Math']>=50].index.tolist() return?
Using the same df, write one line to add Total and one line to select Asha's row with loc.

quiz.a: The double selection may create a copy; assignment hits the copy. Use df.loc[df['Math']>=50,'Total'] = 0.
It splits rows by Class, computes the mean Total in each class, and returns one mean per class.

quiz.q: Tables A(Roll,Name) and B(Roll,Marks) exist. Write a merge that keeps every row of A and adds Marks where Roll matches.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pandas sits inside most Python data pipelines: read a CSV, clean missing values, group by a key, merge lookup tables, then hand numbers to scikit-learn (6.3). Practice with groupby, merge and fillna on a small CSV of your own. Newer libraries such as Polars and Dask copy the DataFrame idea for faster or larger data. Search 'pandas groupby', 'pandas merge' and 'pandas missing data' next.
